To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
trust is a complex concept and that training for decision aids should focus on uncertainty about the aid.
(1) the problem of acceptance is inappropriate trust, and (2) training for decision aid use must address the issue of uncertainty about aid performance.

(a) the problem of decision support system acceptance is not overtrust or undertrust, but rather inappropriate trust; (b) appropriate trust is based on an understanding of the conditions that affect the performance of the decision aid; and (c) this understanding is not easily acquired, and requires special training.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model of trust in decision aids, and its application to the problem of decision aids training.
how people learn to use decision aids.
the problem of trust in decision aids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
trust in decision aids is an issue that is not only important, but also complex and difficult to understand.
the decision aid training is not effective in the real world because it is not designed to deal with the real world.

the problem is neither undertrust (as decision aid proponents claim) nor overtrust (as decision aids skeptics claim), but rather inappropriate trust: a lack of understanding about how to use decision aids effectively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

trust is not an attitude that can be acquired in a few minutes, but an understanding of the conditions under which a decision aid will and will will not perform well that must be acquired in a process of learning.
we need to develop training that is more sensitive to the uncertainty that decision aids introduce.

the training of decision aids must be designed to support the user’s understanding of the uncertainty inherent in the decision aid’s recommendations, so that the user can exploit the aid’s strengths and cope with its weaknesses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
training for decision aids must be designed to help users understand the conditions under which the aid is likely to perform well, and those under which it may not.
the problem of trust in decision aids is neither overtrust nor undertrust, but inappropriate or misplaced trust.
training for the effective use of a decision aid must include training in uncertainty.
